common_name: Russell Hybrid Lupine (Classic Mixed-Color Garden Lupine Strain)

planting.note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. This deep-taprooted plant dislikes transplanting.

directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat, then direct sow into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in fall or early spring. Bred in England by George Russell in the early 20th century from the wild Lupinus polyphyllus, Russell Hybrids remain the classic garden lupine strain, producing dense, densely packed spikes in an exceptional range of colors including blue, purple, pink, red, yellow, white, and striking bicolors, all held above handsome, palmately compound foliage. It thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens and the Pacific Northwest but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it poorly suited to zones 7 and warmer. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a possible second flush of bloom and to control self-seeding, and avoid disturbing the deep taproot once the plant is established.

common_name: The Governor Lupine (Deep Blue and White Bicolor Russell Strain)

planting.note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil.

directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper before sowing, then direct sow into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. The Governor is a long-cultivated named selection from the classic Russell strain of garden lupine, bearing striking bicolor flowers combining deep royal blue standards with crisp white wings on tall, dense spikes above handsome palmately compound foliage. Its bold color contrast has kept it a favorite heirloom lupine selection for generations of cottage gardeners. Like other Russell-type lupines it thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it best suited to zones 7 and cooler. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a possible second flush of bloom, and avoid disturbing the deep taproot once established, since this plant resents transplanting.

The Chatelaine is a long-cultivated named selection from the classic Russell strain of garden lupine, bearing soft bicolor flowers combining rose-pink standards with white wings on tall, dense spikes above handsome palmately compound foliage, a gentler color combination than the more common blues and purples of the genus. Its cottage-garden charm has kept it in cultivation as an heirloom selection for many decades. Like other Russell-type lupines it thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it best suited to zones 7 and cooler. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a possible second flush of bloom, and avoid disturbing the deep taproot once established.

Its intense color makes a strong vertical accent in a cottage or cutting garden border. Like other Russell-type lupines it thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it best suited to zones 7 and cooler. directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper before sowing, then direct sow into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Minarette is a compact, dwarf strain derived from the classic Russell garden lupine, producing the same dense, colorful spikes in a full mix of blues, purples, pinks, reds, yellows, and bicolors, but on a much shorter, sturdier plant that needs little to no staking, unlike the taller full-size Russell strains. Its smaller scale suits container growing, small borders, and front-of-border plantings where taller lupines would be out of proportion. Like other Russell-type lupines it thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it best suited to zones 7 and cooler. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a possible second flush of bloom.
